title: Architecture and Standards: API, Coding, Infra, Model-Serving, Observability, Performance, and ADRs
author: Aisha Patel
body:
Overview

This document consolidates Redwood Inference's canonical architecture and engineering standards across API design, coding practices, infrastructure, model serving, observability, performance targets, and the process for Decision Records (ADRs). It is intended for engineers, architects, and technical product owners who design, build, and operate inference services.

Scope

- Applies to all teams producing and operating services under the Redwood runtime, control plane, and customer-facing APIs.
- Includes hosted, dedicated, and private deployment modes.
- Exclusions: low-risk prototypes and experiments under feature flags (team should still follow guidelines where practical).

Principles

1. Developer-first: APIs and infra should minimize cognitive overhead and make the safe path the easy path.
2. Production-first: default choices prioritize reliability, observability, and predictable economics.
3. Backwards-compatible evolution: breakage is the exception and must be coordinated via ADRs and deprecation schedules.
4. Measurable: every standard includes concrete checks, metrics, and CI gates where possible.

1) API Standards

Purpose: Provide consistent, discoverable, and stable HTTP/REST and RPC interfaces for internal and external consumers.

1.1 Naming and resources
- Use plural nouns for resources (e.g., /v1/models, /v1/inference-requests).
- Version in path (major only): /v1/..., increment major for incompatible changes.
- Prefer predictable query/filter semantics (filtering via query params; complex queries via POST /search).

1.2 HTTP semantics and status codes
- Use 200 for success, 202 for accepted async work, 400 for client errors, 401/403 for auth, 404 for not found, 409 for conflict, 429 for rate-limit, 500/502/503/504 for server / infra errors.
- Include structured error body: {
  "code": "ERROR_CODE",
  "message": "User-friendly message",
  "details": [ ... optional ... ]
}

1.3 Versioning and compatibility
- Additive changes: safe to deploy without version bump.
- Removals or incompatible payload changes: require documented ADR and major version path.
- Deprecation policy: minimum 90 days notice for external APIs; internal APIs follow team agreements but aim for similar notice.

1.4 Authentication & Authorization
- All APIs require authentication (token-based / mTLS depending on surface).
- Use RBAC for service-level authorization; reference roles in docs.

1.5 Pagination and streaming
- Cursor-based pagination (limit + cursor) for list endpoints.
- Server-sent streaming responses for token-generation endpoints (chunked transfer encoding). Provide non-stream fallback.

1.6 Rate limiting & quotas
- Define per-route rate limits and quota tiers in OpenAPI annotations. 429 responses must include Retry-After header.

1.7 Documentation & OpenAPI
- All public and internal-facing APIs must publish an OpenAPI spec in the repo and in the API catalog. Auto-generate SDKs in supported languages.

2) Coding Standards

Purpose: Maintain readability, consistency, and safety across codebases. These are minimum rules — teams may add stricter rules.

2.1 Languages and repositories
- Primary languages: Go (control plane, orchestration), Rust/C++ (hot-path runtime kernels), Python (evals, infra scripts), TypeScript (console).
- Mono-repo or multi-repo is permitted per team; ensure CI can run cross-repo integration tests for service contracts.

2.2 Formatting and linting
- Enforce language standard formatters in pre-commit (gofmt, rustfmt, black, prettier).
- Linting via CI (golangci-lint, clippy, flake8, eslint) with warnings promoted to failures for new code.

2.3 Testing
- Unit tests: target >= 80% coverage for critical services.
- Integration tests: CI stage for API contracts and model-serving smoke tests.
- End-to-end tests: scheduled nightly against a staging environment.
- Must include regression tests for known quality guardrails (e.g., deterministic prompt->response checks for eval harness).

2.4 PR & review process
- Minimum one approver from owning team and one cross-team reviewer for infra or API changes.
- PRs must include description, related ADR (if applicable), and testing notes.
- Use labels: triage/needs-review, type/bugfix|feature|perf, risk/high|medium|low.

2.5 Secrets & keys
- No secrets in source. Use platform secrets (Vault/KMS) and short-lived tokens. CI must scan for accidental secrets.

3) Infrastructure Standards

Purpose: Ensure consistent, secure, and observable infrastructure across deployment modes.

3.1 IaC and environments
- All infra managed with Terraform (modules in infra repo). PRs to infra must include plan outputs.
- Environments: dev, staging, prod. Changes to prod must follow change-management and automated approvals for low-risk changes.

3.2 Image and artifact provenance
- Build artifacts must be signed and stored in an artifact registry. Use SBOMs for runtime images.

3.3 Networking and security
- Zero-trust by default. Use VPC service controls and mTLS between services.
- Public endpoints must be gated by API Gateway, WAF, and rate limiters.

3.4 Capacity & autoscaling
- Use horizontal autoscaling with a documented scaling policy. Dedicated pools (Reserved) must have runbooks for overprovision and burst.

3.5 Backups & recovery
- Define RTO and RPO per service; critical control plane services target RTO < 15m, RPO < 1h. Test restore annually.

4) Model-Serving Standards

Purpose: Standardize how models are packaged, served, rolled out, and monitored to provide predictable latency and quality.

4.1 Model packaging & artifacts
- Canonical formats: support model bundles with metadata manifest (model version, architecture, tokenizer, quantization format). Preferred quant formats: FP16, INT8 (quant profile in manifest).
- All model bundles must include validation checklist and evaluation artifacts (eval datasets + baseline metrics).

4.2 Runtime compatibility & kernels
- Runtime must declare supported ops and fallback compatibility matrix. Kernel selection is automated but teams must provide kernel performance profiles for new model types.

4.3 Caching & batching
- Prefix/KV cache: enable by default for chat sessions. Cache TTLs must be configurable per-route.
- Batching: define batch windows for low-latency vs throughput-heavy routes. Provide safety limits to avoid head-of-line blocking.

4.4 Rollouts & fallbacks
- Canary: start at 1% traffic for 24 hours with health checks.
- A/B experiments and automatic rollback on metric regressions (see observability section).
- Fallback hierarchy: same model older version -> smaller model variant -> degraded feature response. Must be codified in routing policies.

4.5 Quantization & precision standards
- Acceptable quality delta: model quantization must not drop BLEU/ROUGE/LL- eval metrics by more than configured thresholds per workload (default: 2% relative).
- Require offline eval bench and online canary checks for quality drift.

4.6 Security and data handling
- For customer-provided data in private deployments, support KMS/HSM for key management and ensure model artifacts and logs are stored according to data residency requirements.

5) Observability Standards

Purpose: Ensure every service is instrumented for fast detection, triage, and automated action.

5.1 Metrics
- Metrics must follow the Redwood metric schema: <team>.<service>.<resource>.<operation>.<unit>. Examples: ingest.gateway.request_count, runtime.inference.tokens_generated.total.
- Use OpenMetrics semantics and expose /metrics endpoint.
- Required metrics: request_count, success_count, error_count, p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens_generated, cpu_gpu_utilization, batch_size_distribution.

5.2 Tracing
- Distributed tracing via OpenTelemetry. Sample at 1% by default; increase to 100% for canaries or on-demand debug windows.
- Span naming convention: <service>.<operation>. Include model_id and request_id.

5.3 Logs
- Structured JSON logs with severity, request_id, trace_id, tenant_id (if applicable), and tags. Logs must not contain sensitive data (PII). Redaction policies enforced in ingestion.

5.4 Dashboards & Alerts
- Every service must publish a health/dashboard page with: traffic, latency (p50/p95/p99), error rate, capacity utilization.
- Alerting thresholds (examples): error_rate > 0.5% sustained for 5m; p95 latency > 2x baseline for 5m; GPU OOM events > 1/hour.
- Alert routing: PagerDuty for oncall, Slack for SRE/owner. Runbook link in alert annotations.

5.5 SLOs and error budgets
- Define service-level SLOs and detail SLI measurement sources (metrics endpoint + tracing).
- Example SLOs (default for inference API):
  - Availability: 99.95% (monthly)
  - Tail latency (inference route /v1/generate): p95 < 350ms for short-requests (<=128 tokens)
  - Throughput consistency: deploys must not increase 95th-percentile token-cost by > 10% without approval.

6) Performance Standards

Purpose: Provide concrete performance and economics targets and how to measure/validate them.

6.1 Latency targets by route class
- Admin/control-plane APIs: p95 < 100ms
- Model metadata / catalog endpoints: p95 < 200ms
- Inference conversational short requests (<=128 tokens): p95 < 350ms
- Long-generation (>512 tokens): p95 < 2s (depends on model)

6.2 Cost & batching targets
- Batching: configure to maximize GPU utilization while keeping p95 within SLO. Default batching policy: target batch latency budget of 40ms for short requests.
- Default target GPU utilization: 60-80% for Dedicated pools, subject to tail-latency SLOs.

6.3 Benchmarking and perf-suite
- Use standardized benchmarking harness (see benchmarking-and-perf-suite) with representative workloads (chat, instruction, embeddings, long-form).
- Record: latency histograms, memory and GPU utilization, kernel breakdown, and per-token cost. Save results in perf dashboards.

6.4 Performance regressions
- CI must run regression tests for performance-sensitive changes. Regressions >10% relative on p95 latency or >5% on cost-per-token require ADR + rollback plan.

7) ADR (Architecture Decision Record) Process

Purpose: Capture significant architectural decisions, their context, alternatives, and consequences.

7.1 When to create an ADR
- Any decision that affects cross-team contracts, public APIs, deployment topology, data residency/security, or long-term maintainability (examples: change API major version, new kernel ABI, new quantization format).

7.2 ADR template (must be used)
- title: short descriptive title
- status: proposed | accepted | deprecated | superseded
- context: why this decision is necessary
- decision: what we decided to do
- consequences: tradeoffs and follow-ups
- owners: primary and stakeholders
- date: YYYY-MM-DD

7.3 ADR lifecycle
- Draft ADR in repo (adr/ directory) and add link in PRs that implement the change.
- Reviewers: relevant owners and cross-team reviewers.
- Acceptance: consensus and explicit approvals from involved owners; record status and date.
- Deprecation: include migration timeline and compatibility plan.

7.4 Example ADR summary
- title: Adopt GGUF-based quantized model bundles for on-device/inference runtime
- status: accepted
- context: current model packing formats vary across toolchains; GGUF provides a compact, portable format with broad tooling support and explicit metadata fields.
- decision: standardize on GGUF for INT8/INT4 quant bundles at the platform boundary.
- consequences: requires build tooling updates, validation suite, and can increase packaging complexity for certain model families. Rollout: 3-phase migration with canary verification.
- owners: eng-serving-runtime (primary), eng-infra, applied-ml-and-evals.

8) Operational Runbooks & Checklists (summary)

8.1 Pre-deploy checklist
1. Update OpenAPI and publish spec.
2. Add/verify unit & integration tests.
3. Perf regression test against perf-suite.
4. Smoke deploy to staging and run canary traffic.
5. Update dashboards and runbook links.

8.2 Incident triage template
1. Acknowledge & page oncall.
2. Collect key metrics (traffic, error rate, tail latency, GPU utilization).
3. Identify recent deploys or infra events.
4. Escalate to owners and apply rollback/scale actions.
5. Post-incident: write postmortem within 72 hours and link ADRs if architectural changes are required.

9) Ownership and Contacts

- Architecture & standards owner: eng-platform (standards board) - contact: eng-standards@redwood.ai
- API ownership: eng-developer-experience (API working group) - contact: api-team@redwood.ai
- Runtime & kernels: eng-serving-runtime - contact: runtime-team@redwood.ai
- Infra & networking: eng-infra - contact: infra-team@redwood.ai

Appendix A: Example YAML snippets

OpenAPI info example:

openapi: 3.0.1
info:
  title: Redwood Inference API
  version: 1.0.0
paths:
  /v1/generate:
    post:
      summary: Generate text from model
      x-team: runtime
      responses:
        '200':
          description: success

Model manifest example:

---
model_id: gptx-1
version: 2026-02-01
architecture: gpt
quantization: int8-gguf
kernels: [cuda-fp16, cuda-int8]
owner: eng-serving-runtime
quality_baseline:
  perplexity: "24.2"
  rouge_l: "0.41"
---

Appendix B: Table of SLOs and owners (text table)

Service | SLO (monthly) | p95 latency target | Owner
------- | -------------- | ------------------ | -----
Inference API | 99.95% availability | p95 <= 350ms (short) | eng-serving-runtime
Control Plane API | 99.99% availability | p95 <= 100ms | eng-infra
Model Catalog | 99.9% availability | p95 <= 200ms | eng-developer-experience

Appendix C: Rollout checklist (detailed)

1) Prepare ADR and public docs.
2) Publish canary plan and metric checks.
3) Start with 1% traffic for 24 hours. Monitor health & quality.
4) Gradually increase to 10% over 48 hours, then 50% over 48 hours.
5) Full release after 7-day stability window with zero quality regressions.
